title: A moving-frame plot: how does it look from the rotating frame?
summary: The same motion is drawn twice, in a fixed (inertial) frame and in a frame that turns at constant rate. A straight line in the inertial frame becomes a looping curve in the rotating one, which is where the Coriolis and centrifugal effects come from.

media.alt: Two side-by-side plots with a time colour bar. Left: a straight line of dots from lower left to upper right, labelled inertial frame. Right: a looping curve of dots, starting at the same square, labelled rotating frame with the note that it is a curved path with an apparent force.
media.caption: Reference render of class F4.9 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: How does it look from the rotating frame?
read_the_figure.axes: Both panels: x and y in metres, equal scale, -3.5 to 3.5, sharing the vertical axis. Dots every 0.3 s coloured by time (colour bar, 0 to 6 s). Square: the start (-2, -1.5). Pink plus: the origin and rotation axis. Right panel: coordinates in a frame turning at 1 rad/s, aligned with the left frame at t = 0.
look_at: What is the path in each frame, and what is the same in both?
How does the spacing of the dots (the speed) compare between the frames?
What happens near the origin in the right panel, and why?
Which way does the path turn in the rotating frame compared with the frame's own spin?
as_drawn: The body moves in a straight line at constant velocity (0.8, 0.55) m/s (speed 0.97 m/s) from (-2, -1.5), passing within 0.10 m of the origin at t = 2.5 s. No force acts in the inertial frame.
Distances from the origin are identical in both panels; only direction changes. The small loop in the right panel appears when the body is close to the axis.

The note 'apparent force' on the right is the label to read with care: Coriolis and centrifugal terms are not real forces but result from the frame's acceleration. The two panels share the y axis, so tick labels are on the left only.
read_the_figure.proves: That the motion's appearance depends on the frame while the physics (no force in the inertial frame) does not. It does not show the apparent forces as vectors.
if_wrong: The frames' origin and orientation at t = 0 not stated: the right panel cannot be reproduced.
No time encoding: the speed along the path is unreadable.
A rotating frame plotted with unequal axis scales: loops appear distorted.

terms.meaning: A frame in which a force-free body moves in a straight line at constant speed.
A frame that turns with constant angular velocity about an axis.
An apparent acceleration, perpendicular to the velocity, felt in a rotating frame.
An apparent outward acceleration proportional to the distance from the axis.
A term that appears in the equation of motion because of the frame, not because of an interaction.
The matrix that turns a vector by an angle.

remember: Rotating frame position: r' = R(-Omega t) r.
Free body: a' = -2 Omega x v' + Omega^2 r' (in the plane, Omega along z).
Lengths are frame-independent for a rotation; directions change.
State the frame's axis and its alignment at t = 0.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Two side-by-side panels with the same axes. The dots carry time by colour, so you can compare when the body is where in each frame; a square marks the start; a plus marks the origin where the rotation axis passes. Equal scale and shared axes make the panels directly comparable.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A frame is a choice of axes; the body's path is not. Drawing the same trajectory in two frames separates what is real (the body is force-free) from what comes from the viewpoint (the loops). Seeing the straight line become a curve gives the reader the feel for apparent forces without any algebra.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A curved path in the rotating frame is easily read as a real force. The picture does not show which frame is inertial unless you say. A different rotation centre or phase gives a different curve. With equal-time dots the spacing is visible, but without them speed is invisible. And the apparent forces' sizes are not shown.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Both frames side by side is the whole point: a single panel would not be a comparison. Equal axes and the same time colouring make sure the two panels describe one motion.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Overlay both on one plot with the rotating axes drawn at several times. Animate the rotation of the frame. Plot r(t) and the angle in polar form, where the rotating frame subtracts Omega t from the angle. Plot the Coriolis and centrifugal accelerations against time.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Draw the rotating frame's x and y axes as short arrows at t = 0, 2, 4, 6 s on the inertial panel, and the apparent-force vectors on the rotating panel.

steps.title: Moving into the rotating frame
steps.note: With r(t) = (-2, -1.5) + (0.8, 0.55) t and Omega = 1 rad/s the length of r is the same in both panels to 1e-15; only its direction turns by minus Omega t.

steps.title: Where the apparent forces come from
steps.tex: \begin{aligned}\mathbf a'&=\mathbf a-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v'-\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r')\\[4pt]\mathbf a=0:\ \ a'_x&=2\Omega v'_y+\Omega^{2}x',\qquad a'_y=-2\Omega v'_x+\Omega^{2}y'\end{aligned}
steps.note: In the plane with Omega along z. A finite-difference acceleration of the rotating-frame path agrees with this formula to 3e-7. The first term (Coriolis) turns the path, the second (centrifugal) pushes outward from the axis.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) what is the path in each frame? (2) How close does the body come to the origin? (3) Why is the right path curved?

solution.text: Left: a straight line at constant speed (0.97 m/s, the dots are evenly spaced). Right: a looping curve whose dots bunch near the origin and spread far from it: the speed seen in the rotating frame, |v - Omega x r|, is not constant and grows with distance from the axis.
About 0.1 m at t = 2.5 s: the loop in the right panel hugs the origin there.
Because the frame turns: relative to axes spinning at 1 rad/s a force-free body appears to be deflected sideways (Coriolis) and pushed out (centrifugal), although no force acts in the inertial frame.

worked.answer: Straight line (left), loops (right); closest approach about 0.1 m; the curvature is an effect of the rotating frame, not of a force.

evaluate.q: A weather map shows storms curving. Is it 'a force' that curves them? How does the choice of frame matter?

checks.q: What is the path of a force-free body in an inertial frame?
checks.answer: A straight line at constant speed.

checks.q: A frame turns at 1 rad/s. A body is at distance 2 m from the axis. What is the centrifugal acceleration term?
Why do distances from the axis agree in both panels while directions differ?
checks.answer: A rotation of the frame preserves lengths and changes only angles, so |r'| = |r| at all times.
